tagline: Indexes, AI stocks, interest rates, and the eternal question: what are you buying?
why: Everyone in Hong Kong has an opinion on the market, from the Hang Seng to US tech stocks. Investing talk is about what's going up, what the central banks will do, and whether something is a bubble. You don't need to give advice; you just need to understand the vocabulary, the big names and the main schools of thought so you can follow along and ask good questions.

essentials.title: Stocks, bonds and funds
essentials.body: A stock is a slice of a company. A bond is a loan to a government or company that pays interest. Funds and ETFs bundle many of them together.

essentials.title: Indexes measure the market
essentials.body: The S&P 500 (500 big US companies), Nasdaq (tech-heavy), Dow Jones, and in Hong Kong the Hang Seng Index (HSI). 'The market is up' usually means one of these.

essentials.title: Interest rates move everything
essentials.body: When central banks like the US Federal Reserve raise rates, borrowing costs rise and stocks often fall. Cuts usually help stocks and property. Hong Kong's rates follow the US because of the currency peg.

essentials.title: Passive vs active
essentials.body: Passive investors buy cheap index funds and hold. Active investors pick stocks or pay managers to try to beat the market, which most fail to do after fees.

essentials.title: The AI trade
essentials.body: Since 2023, a few giant US tech companies, especially Nvidia, have driven much of the market's gains on AI enthusiasm. Whether it's a bubble is the debate of the moment.

essentials.title: Risk and diversification
essentials.body: Don't put all your eggs in one basket. Spreading money across assets and regions reduces the chance of a big loss.

essentials.title: Valuation
essentials.body: The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio compares a share price to profits. High P/E means investors expect strong growth, or the stock is expensive.

jargon.meaning: A rising market (bull) or one that has fallen 20% or more (bear).
Exchange-traded fund: a basket of investments traded like a stock. The Tracker Fund (2800) follows the Hang Seng.
A fund that simply copies an index. Cheap and popular.

names.name: Warren Buffett
names.what: The most famous investor ever, who built Berkshire Hathaway. Handed the CEO role to Greg Abel at the end of 2025.

names.name: Nvidia
names.what: AI chip maker that became the world's most valuable company, passing $4 trillion and then $5 trillion in 2025.

names.name: Apple and Microsoft
names.what: Two of the largest companies on earth and fixtures in every portfolio.

names.name: Tencent
names.what: Hong Kong's biggest listed company by value: WeChat, gaming and investments.

names.name: Alibaba
names.what: Chinese e-commerce and cloud giant, listed in Hong Kong and New York; rebounded on its AI push.

names.name: HSBC
names.what: The bank founded in Hong Kong in 1865, a dividend favourite for local investors.

names.name: Xiaomi
names.what: Phone and EV maker whose shares soared in 2024-25.

names.name: HKEX
names.what: Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing, which runs the stock market.

names.name: Jerome Powell
names.what: Chair of the US Federal Reserve through May 2026.

names.name: Vanguard
names.what: The firm that popularised low-cost index funds; founder Jack Bogle.

names.name: BlackRock
names.what: The world's largest asset manager, behind iShares ETFs.

names.name: Cathie Wood
names.what: ARK Invest founder known for big bets on disruptive tech.

names.name: Ray Dalio
names.what: Founder of Bridgewater, the biggest hedge fund, known for 'All Weather' investing.

timeline.event: Wall Street crash starts the Great Depression.
The Hang Seng Index is launched.
Black Monday: global markets crash; Hong Kong's exchange closes for four days.
Asian Financial Crisis; Hong Kong defends its currency peg.
The global financial crisis after Lehman Brothers collapses.
Covid crash and rapid recovery; retail trading booms.
Rates rise fast to fight inflation; stocks and bonds both fall.
ChatGPT sparks the AI stock boom.
US 'Liberation Day' tariffs crash markets in April, then a strong rebound; Hong Kong becomes the top IPO venue.

now.headline: The big AI week
now.detail: Nvidia reports on Tuesday 17 November, its first results without Jensen Huang, with analysts expecting about US$109 billion in revenue. Anthropic is expected to start trading on Nasdaq on Thursday 19 November.

now.headline: Anthropic's giant float
now.detail: At US$70-78 a share, Anthropic and some investors aim to raise up to US$64.4 billion by selling 825 million shares, valuing it at up to about US$1.4 trillion.

now.headline: Nvidia after Huang
now.detail: CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO after Huang resigned on 12 November; Nvidia's market value has fallen from about US$5.8 trillion in early October to roughly US$4 trillion.

now.headline: Fed hike coming?
now.detail: Hot October inflation has markets pricing a quarter-point hike on 8-9 December; Fed minutes come out on Wednesday and the 10-year yield is about 5.15%.

now.headline: Hang Seng down three days running
now.detail: The HSI fell 1.55% to 23,637.60 on 13 November, with Tencent down 3.2%. Tencent, Alibaba, Baidu and JD.com all report this week.

now.headline: New World's rights issue
now.detail: New World Development plans a HK$25 billion rights issue after Bain Capital walked away from a possible investment.

local.headline: Everyone trades
local.detail: Hong Kong has a strong retail trading culture. Apps like Futu (Moomoo) are hugely popular.

local.headline: The peg
local.detail: The Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the US dollar between 7.75 and 7.85 since 1983, so local rates follow US rates.

local.headline: MPF
local.detail: The Mandatory Provident Fund is everyone's retirement account. Complaining about MPF fees and returns is a classic topic.

local.headline: Deposit rates
local.detail: When rates were high, many people parked cash in time deposits at 4% or more. Lower rates sent them back to stocks.

local.headline: Dividend stocks
local.detail: HSBC, CLP, HK Electric, Link REIT and the Tracker Fund are traditional local favourites.

debates.question: Index funds or stock picking?
debates.sides: Data says most stock pickers lose to the index; pickers say research and conviction pay.

debates.question: US or China/Hong Kong stocks?
debates.sides: The US has the tech giants; HK and China are cheaper with more upside, but more political risk.

debates.question: Is now a good time to invest?
debates.sides: Long-term investors say time in the market beats timing the market.

debates.question: Gold, property or stocks?
debates.sides: Each has had its moment. Diversifiers say own a bit of everything.
